incomes rise very slowly, while living costs and asset prices keep climbing. That creates a widespread feeling among young South Koreans
even if you study hard, get a decent education, and work diligently, the life your parents' generation achieved seems to be
moving further and further out of reach. Buying a house is harder. Building wealth is harder. And the gap just keeps
widening. Against that backdrop, financial markets start to look extremely attractive. It isn't simply that people want to get rich quickly
Many feel that they don't have many other choices. If wages grow more slowly than asset prices, working hard no longer
seems like enough. You start looking for other paths. The stock market begins to look like a shortcut, and margin trading
is like being handed a faster motorcycle to take down that shortcut. But greater speed also means greater risk. Young South
Koreans have a telling way of describing this feeling: the sense of being left behind. Everything around them seems to
be accelerating—home prices, asset prices, and the wealth of people who already own assets—while they themselves remain stuck in
the same place. When that feeling spreads across an entire generation, it begins to shape financial decisions. People jump into the
market after reading a few investment books, or simply because they feel that time is chasing them. House prices are chasing
them. Living expenses are chasing them. And if they don't run faster, the gap will only get bigger. But that is
only half the story. The other half lies in the structure of South Korea's stock market. One unusual feature of the
South Korean market is the enormous role played by individual investors. In many developed markets, much of the daily trading comes
from investment funds, banks, and large financial institutions. Retail investors are still there, of course, but they are not usually the
main force determining short-term market trends. In South Korea, however, individual investors have accounted for a large share of market turnover
for years. In 2020, they represented roughly two-thirds of trading volume. Even in 2026, their share has frequently hovered around 60
In other words, about six out of every ten trades come from individual investors. That is a very high proportion, and
it has an important consequence: when retail investors get excited, huge amounts of money can rush into the market. When they
panic, selling pressure can arrive just as quickly. The market therefore becomes especially sensitive to crowd psychology. South Koreans even have
